text: I have never been this angry in my life. He hit my mother. I am shaking so hard I can barely hold the pen.
They kept my brother in a cell overnight for something he didn't do and nobody will tell us anything. I could tear the building down.
Found out my business partner has been stealing from the company for three years. Everything I built. I want to scream until my lungs give out.
The driver who killed Sam's dog laughed out of his window as he drove off. I've never felt rage like it.
The school covered up what that teacher did to my daughter. I am incandescent. I will not stop until someone answers for it.
My ex turned up at the kids' school drunk and screamed at me in front of every parent. I am beyond furious.
Pure rage. The landlord changed the locks while we were at work. Our things are inside. The baby's medicine is inside.
Mildly irked that the café gave me oat milk instead of normal. Drank it anyway.
Ambulance came for Dad at 3am. They took him to resus and won't let me in. I can't breathe. I can't stop shaking.
Leo hasn't come home and his phone is off and it's two in the morning. I've called everyone. I'm sick with fear.
The biopsy results are tomorrow at nine. I haven't slept, haven't eaten, haven't stopped pacing. Every minute is an hour.
Lost Mia at the festival for forty minutes. Forty minutes. Found her at the lost-children tent eating a lolly. I'm still trembling.
The plane dropped so suddenly people screamed. I was gripping the seat in front so hard my nails broke. Landed an hour ago and I'm still shaking.
Slightly nervous about tomorrow's dentist check-up. Nothing major.
Everything is falling at once. Mum's in hospital, the house flooded, I lost my job and the kids are terrified. I can't hold any of it.
Sat on the kitchen floor for an hour unable to move. Too many things, too many people, too much. Nothing left in me.
The funeral, the will, the house, the debts, the phone calls. All mine to sort. I'm going under.
Exams, the eviction notice, Dad's diagnosis and my own surgery, all in one fortnight. I can't think. I can barely see.
Launch day disaster. Servers down, investors on the phone, press asking questions, team in tears. I hid in the stairwell and couldn't stop shaking.
Twins in hospital with bronchiolitis, Grandma visiting from abroad, work threatening a disciplinary. I don't know which way is up.
Christmas with forty relatives in a three-bedroom house. I have hidden in the shed. I may live here now.
Seven different people needed me between nine and ten this morning and I said yes to all of them. I'm drowning.
WE WON THE LOTTERY. Not the big one. But enough to clear the mortgage. I'm jumping on the bed at 47 years old.
She said yes. On the beach, at sunset, with the ring I nearly dropped in the sand. I can't stop screaming into my pillow.
I got into Juilliard. JUILLIARD. Mum and I ran around the garden shrieking like children.
Flying out tomorrow to meet my birth mother for the first time. Haven't slept. Can't sit still. Twenty-nine years.
The band is signed! A real record deal! Kofi cried, Jas fainted (a bit), I screamed in a car park.
Two hours until the baby arrives by C-section. We've waited six years for this. I'm vibrating.
Tickets to the World Cup final!!! Uncle Moe had a spare. I've been screaming for an hour.
The publisher wants the trilogy. All three books. I've had to lie down on the floor.
Mildly looking forward to the long weekend. Might paint the fence.
A small flicker of excitement about the new series starting next month.
Quietly looking forward to the farmers' market on Saturday.
I carried the Olympic torch through my home town today. My whole street came out. I've never been so proud in my life.
Watched my son, who they said would never walk, cross the stage at his graduation on his own two feet. I'm undone.
Defended my PhD. Seven years, a divorce and a cancer scare later. Doctor Achebe. I keep saying it out loud.
Pulled a stranger out of the river today. The paramedics said she'd have drowned. My hands won't stop shaking but I'm so glad I jumped.
First in my family to own a house. Signed the papers today with Grandma's pen. I'm so proud I could burst.
Ran the ultra. 100km. 19 hours. Crawled the last mile but crossed the line. I am a different person now.
A tiny bit pleased with how the bread turned out. Nothing to write home about.
Not a single person knows I exist this week. Not one message, not one knock, not one voice. It feels like being erased.
Fifth Christmas alone. I set the table for one, ate in silence and cried into the gravy. I don't think anyone would notice if I vanished.
Since Mariam died there's no one left who knew me before. The loneliness is like a weight on my chest every hour of the day.
In a city of eight million people and I haven't had a real conversation in a month. The isolation is crushing me.
Everyone has someone. I have a phone that never rings and a flat that echoes. It's unbearable tonight.
Locked down alone for six weeks. I've started talking to the radio like it's a person. I'm so desperately lonely.
A touch lonely this evening. Nobody around. It'll pass.
Slightly missed having company at dinner. Fine though.
We buried our daughter today. She was four. I don't know how to keep breathing.
Twenty-five years together and she's gone. I sat in the car outside the hospital and howled.
The vet said there's nothing more they can do for Luna. I held her while she went. My heart is in pieces.
Lost the baby at twenty weeks. We'd already painted the room. I can't stop crying.
The donor family wrote to us. Their son's heart is beating in my husband's chest. I'll never be able to thank them enough.
A stranger gave Mum CPR in the supermarket until the ambulance came. She's alive because of him. I'm overwhelmed with gratitude.
My whole community raised the money for Kai's surgery in three days. Three days. I have no words for how thankful I am.
The firefighters went back into the house for the dog. Everyone's alive. I hugged every single one of them.
Clean scan after two years of treatment. Thank you to every nurse, every doctor, every friend who drove me to chemo. Thank you.
The judge granted us asylum. After four years. I fell to my knees in the courtroom and thanked our lawyer, Mrs. Osei, through my tears.
Slightly grateful the rain held off for the school run.
Small thanks to the bus driver who waited. Nice touch.
A quiet bit of thankfulness for a warm cup of tea.
Thirty hours awake. Two emergency surgeries and a ward with no doctors. I can't feel my hands. I'm so exhausted I'm hallucinating shadows.
Three weeks of newborn twins, maybe ten hours of sleep in total. I can barely stand. I'm crying from tiredness.
Ran on no sleep for four days covering for the whole team. My body is shutting down.
Drove fourteen hours through the night to get to Gran in time. Made it. Now I'm so tired I can't see straight.
Glandular fever. Sleeping eighteen hours a day and still too exhausted to lift a cup.
Finished the harvest at 3am. Every bone aches. I could sleep for a month.
Bit sleepy after lunch. Nothing a coffee won't fix.
Slightly tired, a lazy kind of tired. Nice sofa evening.
A little drowsy from the antihistamines. Nothing major.
Yawned through the afternoon meeting. Early night probably.
After eight years of rejections, I'm so done with this industry I could set fire to my CV. Every door, slammed.
Three months fighting the bank's computer system that keeps freezing my account. I am at the absolute end of my rope.
Tried the recipe nine times. Still collapses. I threw the whole tray against the wall. I'm done with baking forever.
Slightly annoyed the parcel came a day late. No big deal.
The trial results came back: the treatment is working. For the first time in two years I can see a future with my children grown up.
The court has given me the kids back. Supervised at first but they're coming home. I've never felt hope like this.
He opened his eyes today after eleven days in a coma. Squeezed my hand. The doctors are cautiously optimistic and so am I, with every cell of me.
Donor match found for Ana. A real chance. I keep reading the message over and over.
Faint hope the rain clears by Saturday. Probably won't.
Bit of hope the new job ad might be a fit. Will look later.
Mildly optimistic about the garden this year.
Small hope that the café reopens. Liked that place.
Faintly hopeful the train is on time tomorrow.
Took the bins out. Watered the plants.
Meeting at 10, lunch at 1, dentist at 4.
Read the paper. Did the crossword. Went for a walk.
Cooked rice and lentils. Ate. Washed up.
Changed the lightbulb in the hall. Ordered more printer paper.
Drove to the garden centre for compost. Twenty minutes each way.
Phoned the insurance about renewal. They'll email the quote.
Worked from the library today. Wifi was fine.
Swapped the winter duvet for the summer one.
Collected the parcel from the depot. Signed for it.
Defrosted the freezer. Took about an hour.
Booked train tickets for the 14th. Seat reservations included.
Neither up nor down today. Just steady.
Pleasant enough afternoon. Bit of reading, bit of sun.
Mildly content. Nothing to complain about.
Nice enough lunch with the team. Sandwiches in the park.
A small, decent day. Got the washing dry.
Fairly satisfied with the tidy-up. Desk is clear.
Okay day. Small pleasures: good coffee, sunny walk.
Bit cosy tonight. Blanket, film, nothing pressing.
Quietly satisfied with the week. Got through the list.
Mild sense of things being in order.
Soft, unremarkable evening. That suits me.
Bit calmer than yesterday.
Slightly settled after the walk.
Mildly relaxed. Nothing much on.
A faint, peaceful feeling after the rain.
Easy-going morning. No rush.
Quietish day. Mind not racing for once.
Little bit of stillness before bed.
Faintly at ease today.
Passing thought about how fast the kids are growing.
Idly wondering whether to change jobs one day.
Mild musing on the train about where I'll be in ten years.
A small thought about Grandma's old garden today.
Briefly considered what I'd do differently at twenty.
Thinking a little about the book club discussion.
Half-thought about whether I talk too much in meetings.
Pondered the old photos for a minute, then put them away.
A light reflection on the year so far. Mostly fine.
Brief wondering about Dad's choices at my age.
